the choice of a similarity measure for clustering is a tradeoff: the more fine grained the clustering, the more difficult to find the dominant patterns in the data.
the choice of the similarity metric affects the granularity of the detected regularities and thus the regularity patterns captured.

the question of how different definitions of similarity for entities affect the regularities that are detected in ontologies.
the question of which entity similarity function is best suited for detecting regularities in ontological data.
the question of how different similarity functions influence the results of clustering and the detection of regularities.

there is no single similarity measure that is best in every situation.
the choice of a similarity function for clustering is highly dependent on the ontology and the intended use of the regularity detection.
there is no single best similarity measure, as different measures capture regularities of various granularity.

the three similarity functions capture different aspects of similarity and regularities in the ontology and that they are all complementary.
all the variations of similarity are useful for different purposes.

The main takeaway from our work is that

there is no similarity function that is best suited for detecting regularities of all granularity, which means that a similarity function needs to be chosen depending on the granularity of the regularities to be found.
different similarity measures are better suited for detecting different types of patterns.
there are different ways to define pairwise entity similarity and each of these ways leads to a different view of the ontology.
